features: Heavy body, large head, blunt snout, and a whisker-like barbel on the chin. Yellowish-green to reddish or olive with darker speckles, a pale belly, and an easy-to-see lateral line.
habitat: Cold water near the bottom, on rocky slopes and ledges about 30-500 feet deep.

features: Spindle-shaped body that tapers at both ends. Shiny blue-green back with 20 to 30 wavy black bars, and a silvery-white belly. Its colors fade quickly after it dies.
habitat: Cold and temperate ocean water over the continental shelf, swimming in schools near the surface. Young mackerel eat plankton before moving on to larger prey. Caught from May to September.
best_bait: A mackerel tree (a rig with several small lures on one line).

features: Usually black; smaller fish are dusky brown. Dark fins with spots, and white spots and bands on the dorsal fin. Spawning males turn bright blue with a hump on the head.
habitat: Rocky bottoms and structure such as reefs, wrecks, and oyster beds. Moves into coastal waters and bays in spring and offshore in fall. Best fishing is late spring to early summer.

features: Leathery, slippery skin and strong teeth that crush the shells of its prey. Also called tautog, from a Native American name meaning "sheep's head".
habitat: Rocky bottoms, where it feeds on mussels, crabs, clams, and barnacles. Hides among rocks at night and moves to deeper water in winter. Caught from fall, after it moves inshore, until late spring.
best_bait: Crabs or clams on a bottom rig.

features: Sharp teeth and a strong bite, so handle with care. A fast swimmer with good eyesight. Young bluefish are called snappers.
habitat: Travels in large schools in the middle of the water or near the surface. Caught in the surf from late spring to early fall.

features: Usually 5-7 inches long. Bluish gill cover and a black blotch at the back of the soft dorsal fin.
habitat: Warmwater lakes, ponds, and rivers with plenty of weeds or other cover.
best_bait: Worms, artificial flies, or small lures in shallow water near weed beds.

features: Usually 8-20 inches long in inland waters. Many reddish spots on the sides and on the small adipose fin, and a square tail. Originally from Europe.
habitat: Cool streams and lakes. Handles warmer water better than brook trout.
best_bait: Flies, artificial lures, worms, and minnows, cast or trolled.

features: Usually 15-20 inches long. Long, slim body with dark chain-like markings on the sides and back, a dark vertical bar under the eye, and needle-sharp teeth. The smallest member of the pike family.
habitat: Shallow, warm, weedy lakes, where it waits in the weeds to ambush fish and frogs.
best_bait: Minnows, worms, spoons, spinners, and jigs along shallow weed beds. Popular with ice anglers.

features: A large fish, usually 18-28 inches long and sometimes over 40 pounds. Coppery-orange, with a thick spine at the front of the dorsal fin and two barbels (whiskers) on the upper jaw.
habitat: Slow-moving water with a soft bottom in larger lakes and rivers. Often stirs up mud while feeding on plants and small animals.

features: A flatfish with both eyes on one side of its head. It can change color to hide on the bottom.
habitat: Lives on the bottom. Young fish use seagrass beds and tidal marsh creeks. Caught in summer, often by drifting from party, charter, or rented boats.

features: The largest member of the sunfish family, usually 12-18 inches long. Greenish, with a dark band along the side. The upper jaw reaches past the eye.
habitat: Warm, shallow parts of lakes and rivers, among thick weeds or near cover like stumps, logs, and dock pilings.
best_bait: Plastic worms, spinnerbaits, crankbaits, and live bait.

features: Deep-bodied and dusky brown with bright silvery reflections and spiny fins. Has a lot of bones. Also called scup.
habitat: Hard bottoms and submerged structure, and sandy bottoms in large estuaries in summer and early fall. Moves inshore in spring and offshore for the winter. Party boats target it from summer through early fall.

features: Usually 5-7 inches long. Wavy turquoise lines on the head and cheek and a red spot at the tip of the gill cover, but no black blotch on the dorsal fin like a bluegill. New York's most common sunfish.
habitat: Shallow, sheltered water: small lakes and ponds, weedy bays, and slow streams.
best_bait: Worms, small spinners, and jigs in shallow, sheltered water.

features: Usually 10-16 inches long. Coppery-brown body. The upper jaw does not reach past the eye. A hard fighter that often jumps when hooked.
habitat: Cool, clear lakes and streams with gravel or rock bottoms, near rocks and sunken logs.
best_bait: Live bait, spinners, crankbaits, or jigs near rocks, shoals, and other structure.

features: Named for the dark stripes along its sides. Can live up to 30 years.
habitat: Stays close to shore and travels in schools. Lays its eggs in fresh water and estuaries such as the Hudson River. Caught in late spring, summer, and fall.

features: Named for its mouth, which tears easily when hooked. A good fighter on light tackle.
habitat: Caught late in the evening from spring to the start of summer.

features: An oval, thick-bodied flatfish with both eyes on the right side and a straight lateral line. Reddish-brown to olive or nearly black on top, white underneath.
habitat: Shallow bays and estuaries with sand or silt bottoms, often buried except for its eyes. Moves inshore to spawn in winter and spring.

features: Usually 8-12 inches long. Yellow sides with six or seven dark vertical bars.
habitat: Shallow, weedy, protected parts of lakes, ponds, and rivers.
best_bait: Minnows, worms, grubs, and small lures along weed beds and drop-offs. Popular for ice fishing.
